papers.title_in_file: Characterizing Continual Learning Scenarios for Tumor Classification in Histopathology Images
papers.version_note: The text is the arXiv v1 preprint (2208.03609v1, 7 Aug 2022, eess.IV); the running head reads 'Continual Learning for Tumor Classification in Histopathology Images' and the file name matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A MICCAI 2022 style study that defines four continual learning scenarios for histopathology and benchmarks EWC, Online EWC, LwF, iCaRL, A-GEM and CoPE on a stain-augmented colorectal cancer dataset and on CRC plus PatchCam.

assertions.value: The authors define the Data Incremental scenario (Data-IL) as continually learning from new streams of data from an identical underlying distribution during model development or update. They state that Data-IL does not consider new classes or considerable shifts of data distribution and is expected to be the easiest among all CL scenarios.
quotes: Continuously learn from new streams of data from an identical underlying distribution during model development or update.
Data-IL does not consider new classes or considerable shifts of data distribution and is thus expected to be the easiest
among all CL scenarios. In DP, it is common for expert pathologists to generate annotations for a dataset in multiple batches
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines the scenario.
assertions.reader_inference: The expectation that Data-IL is easiest is not borne out for every method: in Table S1 only LwF exceeds finetuning in Data-IL.

assertions.value: The authors define the Domain Incremental scenario (Domain-IL) as continually updating a model with new streams of data from shifted distributions, with examples such as variations of tissue processing/staining reagents, patient populations and scanning instruments. They state that the extent of domain shift is a continuum and that the categorization of a scenario into Data-IL or Domain-IL is a design choice and/or empirical decision.
quotes: Continuously update a model with new streams of data from shifted distributions.
Examples in clinical settings include variations of tissue processing/staining reagents, patient populations, scanning instruments and so on.
the categorization of a scenario into Data-IL or Domain-IL is a design choice and/or empirical decision.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines the scenario.

assertions.value: The authors define the Class Incremental scenario (Class-IL) as continually extending an existing model to unseen classes with new streams of data. They state that, because the knowledge to learn from each batch of unseen classes is largely non-overlapping, this scenario is expected to be the hardest among CL scenarios.
quotes: Continuously extend an existing model to unseen classes with new streams of data.
Since the knowledge to learn from each batch of unseen classes is largely non-overlapping, this scenario is expected to be the hardest among CL scenarios.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines the scenario.

assertions.value: The authors define the Task Incremental scenario (Task-IL) as any of the other scenarios in which each data stream is defined as a new task and prior knowledge of the task identity (task ID) is always given at inference. They state that in this study they tested Task-IL with new classes introduced at each task.
quotes: Any of the above scenarios can be considered as Task-IL if each data stream is deﬁned as a new task
prior knowledge is always given as to which task (task identity, i.e. task ID) the test data should be predicted with.
In this study, we tested the task IL scenario with new classes introduced at each task.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines the scenario and states how it is tested here.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to their best knowledge, there is no systematic study so far on continual learning performance of deep learning or machine learning models designed for histopathology images, and consequently no appropriate CL baselines for digital pathology. They also state that, to the best of their knowledge, no benchmark for simulating CL scenarios had been proposed for digital pathology analysis.
quotes: to our best knowledge, there is no systematic study so far on CL performance on deep learning/machine learning models designed for histopathology images, and consequently, no appropriate CL baselines for DP.
To the best of our knowledge, no such benchmark has been proposed for
assertions.reader_inference: A priority and novelty claim made without a literature search shown in the paper. Reference 19 (Perkonigg et al.) and others in the cited list study CL in medical imaging, but not histopathology.

assertions.value: The authors state that continual learning algorithms have largely been tested on relatively less complex datasets from non-DP domains, including MNIST and CIFAR, and that the insights from these thus cannot be directly transferred to DP data.
quotes: these CL algorithms have largely been tested on relatively less complex datasets from non-DP domains, including MNIST [1, 8, 17]
the insights from which thus cannot be directly transferred to DP data.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not test whether insights from MNIST or CIFAR transfer; the assertion is a premise, not a result.

assertions.value: The authors state that training on all existing and newly arrived data from scratch in general ensures performance but requires storage of all the data and increasing computing resources at each update. They state that updating a model with transfer learning has no extra cost of data storage and computing resources but is known to suffer from catastrophic forgetting.
quotes: Such an approach in general ensures performance, but requires storage of all the data and an increasing amount of computing resources each time a model is updated
updating a model with transfer learning, albeit with no extra cost of data storage and computing resources, is known to suﬀer from catastrophic forgetting [14].
assertions.reader_inference: Motivation for the study. The forgetting claim is attributed to reference 14 (Kirkpatrick et al.).

assertions.value: The authors list three contributions: identifying continual learning scenarios practical for digital pathology analysis and characterizing the performance of recent CL methods in them; establishing an augmented H&E dataset simulating data streams from multiple data sources; and exploring learning continuously from more than one tumor type and applying online CL methods.
quotes: Our contributions are three-fold: (1) we identify continual learning scenarios practical for DP-based analysis
(2) we establish a dataset with augmented H&E images, simulating data streams from multiple data sources
(3) we have explored the feasibility and provided insights into performance of both learning continuously from more than one type of tumor
assertions.certainty_reason: The introduction states the scope of the study.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used a colorectal cancer (CRC) dataset of stain-normalized 224x224 patches at 20x from H&E stained whole-slide images (136 patients) with tile-wise labels for 9 tissue types: tumor, stroma, normal, lymphocyte-rich, mucin, muscle, adipose, debris and background.
quotes: composed of stain-normalized [18] 224x224 patches at 20x from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained wholeslide images (136 patients)
with tile-wise class labels for 9 tissue types - tumor, stroma, normal, lymphocyte-rich, mucin, muscle, adipose, debris, background.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.1 states the dataset used.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to establish a class-balanced dataset, they randomly selected 8700 images from each class for training (7000 train; 2700 validation) and used the entire test set (7150 images) for testing.
quotes: we randomly selected 8700 images from each class for training (7000 train; 2700 validation) and the entire test set (7150 images) for testing.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.1 states the data split used.
assertions.reader_inference: The stated figures do not add up: 7000 plus 2700 is 9700, not 8700. The later text also uses 8700/5 = 1740 examples per class per domain 'for training', which would be 1400 if training were 7000. The paper does not say which figure is the actual training size.

assertions.value: The authors state that PatchCam was used for breast cancer classification, comprising 96x96 patches labeled normal or tumor from 400 breast cancer H&E whole-slide images at 20x resolution, and that they stain-normalized the patches to be consistent with the colorectal cancer dataset.
quotes: PatchCam from [5] was used for breast cancer classiﬁcation, which comprises 96x96 patches with class labels of “normal” and “tumor” from 400 breast cancer H&E whole-slide images at 20x resolution.
We stain-normalized [18] the patches to be consist with colorectal cancer dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.1 states the second dataset used.

assertions.value: The authors state that they simulated domain shifts by creating four additional data sources (Domains 2 to 5) beside the original CRC images (Domain 1). They randomly divided the images of each of the 9 classes into 5 splits, kept 1 split unchanged for Domain 1, and performed stain unmixing on the remaining splits before applying augmentations to remix them into augmented H&E images, called augmented CRC.
quotes: Except for the images provided by CRC (Domain 1), we simulated 4 additional data sources (Domain 2-5)
randomly divided images in each of the 9 classes into 5 splits, kept 1 split unchanged for Domain 1 and performed stain unmixing [21] for the remaining splits.
remix the stain-unmixed intensity images into augmented H&E and refer to this augmented dataset as augmented CRC.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 describes how the augmented dataset was built.

assertions.value: The authors state that Domain 2 (increased stain intensity) was made by randomly increasing eosin intensity with a scaling factor sampled from [1.75, 2.75] and hematoxylin intensity from [1.5, 2.0].
quotes: Domain 2 (increased stain intensity, simulating, for example, concentration increase of the eosin and/or hemotoxylin solutions, each with a diﬀerent extent of change)
eosin intensity was randomly increased with a scaling factor sampled from [1.75, 2.75], hematoxylin from [1.5, 2.0].
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 gives the augmentation settings.

assertions.value: The authors state that Domain 3, described as decreased eosin stain intensity (simulating slides with fading stain), used an eosin intensity scaling factor sampled from [0.4, 2.75].
quotes: Domain 3 (decreased eosin stain intensity, simulating, for example, slides prepared from many years ago with fading stain)
eosin intensity scaling factor sampled from [0.4, 2.75].
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 gives the augmentation settings.
assertions.reader_inference: The range [0.4, 2.75] reaches above 1, so it also covers intensity increases although the domain is described as a decrease; the upper bound 2.75 matches Domain 2's eosin upper bound and may be a typographical error. The paper does not comment.

assertions.value: The authors state that Domain 4 (change of hue) changed eosin hue by a scaling factor sampled from [-0.05, -0.03] and hematoxylin hue from [0.05, 0.08].
quotes: Domain 4 (change of hue, simulating, for example, change of reagent manufacturer, scanner or stainer):
eosin hue changed by a scaling factor sampled from [-0.05, -0.03], hematoxylin from [0.05,0.08].
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 gives the augmentation settings.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 4.1 later describes Domain 4 as 'change of hue and saturation', while Section 3.2 gives hue and saturation changes to Domain 5 only. The two descriptions of Domain 4 differ.

assertions.value: The authors state that Domain 5 (change of hue and saturation) changed eosin hue by [0.03, 0.05], increased saturation for eosin by [1.2, 1.4] and for hematoxylin by [1.1, 1.3].
quotes: Domain 5 (change of hue and saturation, simulating, for example, change of reagent manufacturer, scanner or stainer):
eosin hue changed by [0.03, 0.05]; saturation increased for eosin by [1.2, 1.4] and hematoxylin by [1.1, 1.3].
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 gives the augmentation settings.

assertions.value: The authors report that they presented four randomly selected images from each domain to two pathologists. Both confirmed that images of Domain 1-4 look realistic, and one pathologist thought Domain 5 slightly deviates from the majority of DP images from the authors' organization.
quotes: We presented four randomly selected images from each domain to two pathologists.
Both of them conﬁrmed that images of Domain 1-4 look realistic and one pathologist thought the Domain 5 is slightly deviating from majority of DP images from our organization.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: A qualitative check on a very small sample (four images per domain, two raters); it does not validate realism across the full augmented set.

assertions.value: The authors state that for Domain-IL the 5 domains were used as individual batches of data, each domain containing examples from all 9 classes, giving for training 8700/5 = 1740 examples per class per domain.
quotes: For Domain-IL, the 5 domains were used
as individual batches of data with domain shifts, where each domain contains examples from all 9 classes (e.g. for training, 8700/5 = 1740 examples per class per domain).
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 states the experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: This is in tension with the 7000 training images per class stated in Section 3.1; see crc-class-balanced-subset.

assertions.value: The authors state that in Class-IL each data batch contains all examples from the new classes, with the same number of examples from each domain for each class, and that in Data-IL each data batch was randomly selected and contained roughly the same number of examples from each domain.
quotes: In Class-IL, each data batch contains all examples from the new classes and thus the same number of examples from each domain for each class.
In Data-IL, each data batch was randomly selected and roughly contained the same number of examples from each domain.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 states the experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: Data-IL batches therefore contain all five domains; the Data-IL scenario here is not drawn from a single domain although Section 2 defines it as an identical underlying distribution.

assertions.value: The authors state that recent continual learning methods can be largely classified into replay, regularization and parameter isolation methods, citing reference 28. They state that parameter isolation methods only apply to Task-IL because they require multi-headed designs and use task IDs to select a task-specific head at inference, while replay and regularization apply to all scenarios.
quotes: Recent proposed CL methods can be largely classiﬁed into three categories: replay, regularization and parameter isolation [28].
while replay and regularization apply to all scenarios, parameter isolation only applies to Task-IL
both require multi-headed designs and use task IDs to select a task-speciﬁc head during inference.
assertions.reader_inference: Parameter isolation methods are not evaluated in the paper, consistent with its choice of scenarios.

assertions.value: The authors state that they evaluate EWC, Online EWC, LwF, iCaRL, A-GEM and CoPE. They state that A-GEM was tested in the literature only in Class-IL and Task-IL, and that they tested CoPE in Data-IL, Domain-IL and Class-IL.
quotes: Here we evaluate the following CL methods.
In the literature, A-GEM was tested only in Class-IL and Task-IL scenarios as reported in [8].
We tested CoPE in Data-IL, Domain-IL and Class-IL scenarios.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 lists the methods under test.
assertions.reader_inference: Table S1 reports A-GEM only for Task-IL and Class-IL, CoPE only for Data-IL, Domain-IL and Class-IL, and iCaRL for Data-IL, Domain-IL and Class-IL but not Task-IL.

assertions.value: The authors describe EWC and Online EWC as regularization-based methods whose loss includes a term penalizing large changes to network weights important for previous tasks, proportional to each weight's importance. They state that in EWC the number of quadratic penalty terms grows linearly with the number of tasks, and that Online EWC uses a single quadratic penalty term whose strength is determined by a running sum of parameter importance, with an additional decay hyperparameter.
quotes: The loss function includes a regularization term, which penalizes large changes to network weights that are important for previous tasks
In EWC, the number of quadratic penalty terms grows linearly with the number of tasks.
Online EWC [23] uses a single quadratic penalty term on parameters whose strength is determined by a running sum of parameter importance from previous tasks.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's description of methods proposed in references 14 and 23.

assertions.value: The authors describe LwF as a data-focused regularization method that distills knowledge from a previous model to an updated model trained on new data, replaying each input with a soft target obtained from a copy of the model stored after training on the most recent task.
quotes: Data-focused regularization method [16] which distills knowledge from a previous model to an updated model trained on new data.
Each input is replayed with a soft target obtained using a copy of the model stored after ﬁnishing training on the most recent task.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's description of the method proposed in reference 16.

assertions.value: The authors describe iCaRL as a replay-based method storing a subset of the most representative original images per class in memory, chosen according to approximate class means in the learned feature space, with memory size determined by grid search and/or availability of computing resources.
quotes: Replay-based method using stored original images from previous data streams [20].
which are chosen according to approximate class means in the learned feature space.
The memory size can be determined by grid search and/or availability of computing resources.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's description of the method proposed in reference 20.

assertions.value: The authors describe A-GEM as an online constrained replay-based method in which model updates are constrained to prevent forgetting by projecting the estimated gradient on the direction determined by randomly selected samples from a replay buffer, with buffer size and sampling size from the buffer as tunable hyperparameters.
quotes: In this online constrained replay-based method [8], model updates are constrained to prevent forgetting by projecting the estimated gradient
on the direction determined by randomly selected samples from a replay buﬀer.
Buﬀer size and sampling size from the buﬀer are both tunable hy-
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's description of the method proposed in reference 8.

assertions.value: The authors describe CoPE as an online rehearsal-based approach that enables rapidly evolving prototypes with balanced memory and a loss function that updates the representations or pseudo prototypes, thus alleviating catastrophic forgetting.
quotes: An online rehearsal based approach [10], which enables rapidly evolving prototypes with balanced memory and a loss function that updates the representations or pseudo prototypes
thus alleviating catastrophic forgetting.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's description of the method proposed in reference 10.

assertions.value: The authors define an experience as learning from a batch of data for CL. They report accuracy averaged over test sets at the end of training the last experience from multiple repeats, and accuracy over multiple repeats at each experience. They state that evaluation on test sets from past experiences indicates how well the model retains past knowledge without forgetting (backward transfer), while accuracy on current or future test sets reflects new knowledge assimilation (forward transfer).
quotes: We refer to learning from a batch of data for CL as an experience.
accuracy averaged over test sets at the end of training the last experience from multiple repeats
While evaluation on test sets from past experiences indicates how well the model retains past knowledge without forgetting (backward transfer)
accuracy on current/future test sets reﬂects new knowledge assimilation (forward transfer)
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 defines the evaluation terms and metrics used.

assertions.value: The authors state that all methods were compared against two baselines: joint training (upper bound), where a model was trained on all the data available so far, and finetuning (that is, transfer learning; lower bound), where a model was trained sequentially with exposure to only the data from the current experience. For A-GEM and CoPE they also compared online versions of the baselines: A-GEM baselines trained in an online setup for 1 epoch, and CoPE baselines with experiences divided into mini experiences of 128 samples each, trained for 1 epoch per mini experience.
quotes: 1) joint training (upper bound), where a model was trained on all the data available so far;
2) ﬁnetuning (i.e transfer learning; lower bound), where a model was trained sequentially with exposure to only the data from the current experience.
the A-GEM baselines were trained in an online setup for 1 epoch
the experiences were divided into mini experiences (128 samples each) in a data incremental fashion and trained for 1 epoch per mini experience
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 defines the baselines.
assertions.reader_inference: Joint training is called the upper bound, but in Table S1 LwF in Data-IL (91.32) exceeds Joint (90.48), and Joint (A-GEM) in Task-IL (65.58) is below A-GEM (72.41); the 'bounds' are not strict in the reported results.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used ResNet-18 feature extraction layers followed by a single-layer nearest mean classifier, assigning the class label by the nearest prototype vector. Training used 15 epochs and a batch size of 16 on 1 NVIDIA V100 or A100 GPU for 3-5 repeats, with Stochastic Gradient Descent, learning rate 0.1, momentum 0.9, and a weight decay of 0.00001 applied after epochs 10 and 13. Hyperparameters were found by grid search in all scenarios.
quotes: We used a ResNet-18 [11] feature extraction layers followed by a single-layer nearest mean classiﬁer [20]
Training was conducted with 15 epochs and a batch size of 16 on 1 NVIDIA V100 or A100 GPU for 3-5 repeats.
Models were optimized with Stochastic Gradient Descent starting with a learning rate of 0.1 and momentum of 0.9 and a weight decay of 0.00001 applied after epochs 10 and 13.
In all scenarios we ran grid search for best hyperparameters
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 states the implementation.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence reads as if weight decay is applied after epochs 10 and 13, which may mean a learning-rate decay schedule; the text does not clarify. Each result is a mean over only 3 to 5 repeats.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table S1 mean accuracy ± standard deviation for the Joint baseline of 90.48 ± 5.12 (Data-IL), 89.43 ± 2.15 (Domain-IL), 89.58 ± 5.27 (Task-IL) and 85.94 ± 4 (Class-IL). They state that the accuracy of the joint baseline was comparable across scenarios.
quotes: Overall, the accuracy of joint baseline was comparable across scenarios
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: Standard deviations of 5 points in three of four scenarios mean most pairwise differences among methods in Data-IL and Task-IL lie within one standard deviation. The Class-IL joint value is about 3.5 to 4.5 points lower than the others.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table S1 mean accuracy ± standard deviation for the finetuning baseline of 88.49 ± 3.15 (Data-IL), 61.42 ± 2.55 (Domain-IL), 80.1 ± 5.51 (Task-IL) and 26.61 ± 0.4 (Class-IL). They state that finetuning performance varies among scenarios, with best performance on Data-IL and worst on Class-IL.
quotes: the performance of ﬁnetuning varies among scenarios with best performance on Data-IL and worst on Class-IL
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: The Class-IL finetuning accuracy of 26.61 is consistent with forgetting of all but the latest classes (a 9-class, five-experience setup), but the paper does not give the chance level.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table S1 accuracy ± standard deviation for EWC of 86.77 ± 4.37, 63.64 ± 3.2, 78.41 ± 3.35 and 27.3 ± 0.63; for Online EWC of 83.29 ± 10.02, 67.51 ± 3.07, 76.83 ± 2.64 and 26.79 ± 0.37; for LwF of 91.32 ± 0.83, 66.24 ± 3.57, 80.59 ± 4.95 and 28.88 ± 2.08; and for iCaRL of 80.97 ± 4.51 (Data-IL), 73.41 ± 3.12 (Domain-IL) and 72.06 ± 3.2 (Class-IL), in the order Data-IL, Domain-IL, Task-IL, Class-IL (iCaRL has no Task-IL entry).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: In the text layer the iCaRL row is split across two lines and the Task-IL cell is a dash; the Class-IL value 72.06 is read from the last cell. In Task-IL and Class-IL the LwF differences from finetuning (80.59 against 80.1; 28.88 against 26.61) are smaller than the reported standard deviations.

assertions.value: The authors state that, of the offline CL methods tested, LwF and iCaRL performed much better than finetuning in all scenarios except for Data-IL. They state that the accuracy of EWC and Online EWC was comparable to finetuning in all scenarios except for Domain-IL.
quotes: Of the oﬄine CL methods tested, LwF and iCaRL performed much better than ﬁnetuning in all scenarios
except for Data-IL. Accuracy of EWC/online EWC was comparable to ﬁnetuning in all scenarios except for Domain-IL
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: Table S1 does not support 'much better' for LwF in Task-IL (80.59 ± 4.95 against 80.1 ± 5.51) or in Class-IL (28.88 ± 2.08 against 26.61 ± 0.4), and iCaRL has no Task-IL entry. The statement holds clearly only for iCaRL in Domain-IL and Class-IL and, more weakly, LwF in Domain-IL (66.24 against 61.42).

assertions.value: The authors state that in Domain-IL online EWC was 6.09% higher than EWC.
quotes: where online EWC was 6.09% higher than EWC.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: Table S1 gives Online EWC 67.51 and EWC 63.64 in Domain-IL, a difference of 3.87 points. The figure 6.09 equals the difference between Online EWC (67.51) and finetuning (61.42), so the sentence appears to compare to finetuning rather than EWC.

assertions.value: The authors report that the computation time for the joint baseline was much longer (250 ± 18 minutes) than for CL methods across scenarios (70 ± 8 minutes), and state in the discussion that CL methods took only about 28% of the runtime of joint training.
quotes: the computation time for joint baseline was much longer (250 ± 18 minutes) compared to that of for CL methods across scenarios (70 ± 8 minutes)
CL methods were also computationally eﬃcient, taking only about 28% of the runtime as joint training.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: 70 divided by 250 is 0.28, matching the stated percentage. The paper does not say whether the times are per run, per method, or averaged over methods, nor whether hyperparameter search is included.

assertions.value: The authors report that in Data-IL only LwF (accuracy 91.32%) outperformed finetuning, and state that this was 2.87% higher than the upper bound joint training. They report that iCaRL, the best method in the other scenarios, was 7.52% lower than finetuning in Data-IL.
quotes: we found that only LwF (accuracy: 91.32%) outperformed ﬁnetuning and even 2.87% higher than the upper bound joint training.
While iCaRL was the best method for other scenarios, it was 7.52% lower than ﬁnetuning.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: Table S1 gives Data-IL Joint 90.48, so LwF (91.32) is 0.84 points above it, not 2.87; 91.32 minus finetuning (88.49) is 2.83. iCaRL (80.97) is 7.52 below finetuning (88.49), which matches. LwF exceeds finetuning by less than finetuning's standard deviation (3.15).

assertions.value: The authors state that iCaRL was designed and tested for Class-IL with replay memory divided equally across classes, and that in their Data-IL setting the allocated memory for each class was split further across the five domains. They state a hypothesis that a bigger memory with more examples per class per domain could have produced better results.
quotes: iCaRL was designed and tested for Class-IL in [20] and the replay memory was divided equally to store examples from each class.
In our Data-IL setting, the allocated memory for each class was split further for each of the ﬁve domains.
We hypothesized a bigger memory with more examples for each class per domain could have produced better results.
assertions.reader_inference: The hypothesis is not tested in the paper; memory sizes used are not stated in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that in Domain-IL iCaRL achieved the best accuracy of 73.41%, and state that while other methods show a reduction in performance after learning Domain 2 and 4, the performance of iCaRL continued to improve (Fig. 2).
quotes: In Domain-IL, iCaRL achieved the best accuracy of 73.41%.
while other methods show a reduction in performance after learning Domain 2 and 4, the performance of iCaRL continued to improve (Fig. 2)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: The per-experience curves are in a figure not available in the text layer; the value rests on the stated sentence. Table S1 gives 73.41 ± 3.12 for iCaRL against 89.43 ± 2.15 for Joint in Domain-IL.

assertions.value: The authors state that Domain 1 and Domain 4 showed minimal forgetting (Fig. S2), while Domains 2 and 3 with eosin intensity changes were much harder for CL. They suggest that intensity changes in practice, due for example to scanner differences, may lead to larger challenges for CL than hue/saturation changes, and state that Domains 2 and 3 were the farthest from baseline DP settings in appearance.
quotes: Domain 1 (original stain-normalized images) and Domain 4 (change of hue and saturation)
showed minimal forgetting (Fig. S2), while Domains 2 and 3 with eosin intensity changes were much harder for CL
suggesting that intensity changes in practice due to, for example, scanner differences, may lead to larger challenges for CL than hue/saturation changes
These 2 domains were the farthest from baseline DP settings in appearance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: The same passage labels Domain 4 'change of hue and saturation', whereas Section 3.2 defines Domain 4 as hue only. The sentence also mentions forgetting after Domain 4 for most methods (domain-il-icarl-best), which sits in tension with 'minimal forgetting' for Domain 4. Domains 2 and 3 are also the domains with the largest augmentation ranges, so intensity and magnitude of shift are confounded.

assertions.value: The authors state that the five domains were designed to have relatively large domain gaps with non-overlapping augmentation settings, and that in practice, by performing stain normalization during model training or for datasets with smaller domain shifts, the domain gaps would be reduced and CL performance potentially improved.
quotes: Note that here the 5 domains were designed to have relatively large domain gaps with non-overlapping augmentation settings
by performing stain normalization during model training or for datasets with smaller domain shifts, the domain gaps would be reduced and thus potentially improving CL performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope and a limit of its own augmented benchmark here.
assertions.reader_inference: The improvement from stain normalization is not tested; the data were already Macenko stain-normalized before augmentation (Section 3.1).

assertions.value: The authors state that in Task-IL finetuning accuracy was much higher than in Class-IL, which they say was likely due to the presence of task-specific network modules and additional information (task IDs) used during inference.
quotes: In Task-IL, ﬁnetuning accuracy was much higher than that of Class-IL, likely due to the presence of task-speciﬁc network modules and additional information leveraged (taks IDs) during inference.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: Table S1: finetuning 80.1 ± 5.51 in Task-IL against 26.61 ± 0.4 in Class-IL. The explanation is the authors' and is not tested by an ablation.

assertions.value: The authors state that in Task-IL, unlike what references 19, 27 and 28 have reported, LwF was the only method that performed better than finetuning. They say this could be because in their network design task identities were only used in the output layer, while embedding task identities in hidden layers was reported to be more effective.
quotes: However, unlike [19, 27, 28] have reported, LwF was the only method that performed better than ﬁnetuning (Fig. 1 Right and S3).
This could be because in our network design task identities were only used in the output layer, while it was reported to be more eﬀective to embed task identities in hidden layers [10].
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: Table S1 Task-IL: LwF 80.59 ± 4.95, finetuning 80.1 ± 5.51, EWC 78.41 ± 3.35, Online EWC 76.83 ± 2.64. The LwF advantage of 0.49 is far inside the standard deviation. The mechanism offered is a hypothesis; no hidden-layer task-ID variant was run.

assertions.value: The authors state that Class-IL is the most difficult learning scenario and that, as expected, most methods suffered from severe forgetting of previous knowledge. They report that iCaRL had the best overall accuracy of 72.06% with a random ordering of classes (Fig. S4), and state that this is consistent with reference 27 that replay methods are more effective in Class-IL than regularization methods.

iCaRL had the best overall accuracy of 72.06% when tested with a random ordering of classes (Fig. S4).

assertions.reader_inference: The text layer flattens Table S2; values are matched to labels by order (the grouping row lists three means and three standard deviations separately). The 9-class entry 46.55 ± 1.89 equals the grouping:333 entry, and the main Class-IL result 72.06 ± 3.2 equals the grouping:2223 entry, so the table does not make clear which setting is the main experiment. The class-order spread (68.57 to 81.11) is larger than the Class-IL differences among non-replay methods, so class order is a substantial uncontrolled factor. The curriculum interpretation is the authors' and is not tested directly.

assertions.value: The authors state that A-GEM outperformed the online joint baseline for A-GEM in Task-IL by 6%, but suffered from catastrophic forgetting without task identity. They report in Table S1 A-GEM accuracy of 72.41 ± 1.81 (Task-IL) and 21.62 ± 3.45 (Class-IL), against finetuning (A-GEM) of 64.93 ± 9.13 and 19.57 ± 7.35 and Joint (A-GEM) of 65.58 ± 13.19 and 90 ± 2.72 in the same scenarios.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.1, p.8; Fig. 3 left; Table S1, p.12
quotes: A-GEM outperformed the online joint baseline for A-GEM (Fig. 3 Left) in Task-IL by 6%, but suﬀered from catastrophic forgetting without task identity.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: 72.41 minus 65.58 is 6.83 points, not 6. The Joint (A-GEM) Task-IL value (65.58 ± 13.19) is lower than the Joint (A-GEM) Class-IL value (90 ± 2.72) and has a very wide standard deviation, so the 'upper bound' comparison is noisy. The Class-IL A-GEM figure (21.62) is within the standard deviation of its finetuning baseline (19.57 ± 7.35).

assertions.value: The authors state that CoPE was worse than finetuning in Data-IL and Class-IL, but 6% better in Domain-IL (Fig. 3 Right), and that knowledge retention (backward transfer) with CoPE was much better in Data-IL and Domain-IL despite lower performance compared to offline methods. They report in Table S1 CoPE accuracy of 82.16 ± 4.63 (Data-IL), 66.71 ± 2.49 (Domain-IL) and 19.15 ± 6.16 (Class-IL), against finetuning (CoPE) of 84.92 ± 4.41 (Data-IL) and 60.85 ± 6.04 (Domain-IL).

assertions.value: The authors state that CoPE was sensitive to softmax temperature and that further finetuning could help improve forward transfer. They state that the online results demonstrate that online CL poses challenges, which calls for more attention in research.
quotes: We note that CoPE was sensitive to softmax temperature and further ﬁnetuning could help improve forward transfer.
demonstrating that online CL poses challenges, which calls for more attention in research
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: The temperature sensitivity is reported without numbers or a sweep in the text; whether the CoPE results were tuned for temperature is not stated.

assertions.value: The authors report testing a dramatic domain shift by training with the original CRC images in one experience and the PatchCam dataset in another, using LwF in a Domain-IL setting with each tumor type as one domain, and varying the order of the domains and the volume of PatchCam data. They state that joint baseline accuracy was around 80%, and that LwF performed better than finetuning when PatchCam was introduced first, followed by CRC.
quotes: We tested a dramatic domain shift in data streams by training a model with the original CRC images in one experience and PatchCam dataset in another experience.
We experimented with LwF for continually learning the two datasets in a Domain-IL setting, where each tumor type is considered as one domain.
As shown in Fig. 4, joint baseline accuracy was around 80%.
LwF performed better than ﬁnetuning when PatchCam was introduced ﬁrst during training followed by CRC in the subsequent experience.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: Only LwF was tested in this experiment, and only two orders and two data ratios.

quotes: As expected, including 3 times more data in training improved accuracy by over 11% (Table S2).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with 3 to 5 repeats.
assertions.reader_inference: From Table S2, the over-11 figure matches only LwF in the CAM-first order (65.48 to 76.57, a gain of 11.09). For the same increase in CRC/CAM order, LwF gains 3.45 (76.39 to 79.84), finetuning 2.2 and Joint 2.58. The statement does not say which comparison it refers to, so it is order- and method-specific.

assertions.value: The authors state that, although regularization-based methods performed well in Data-IL and Domain-IL, only iCaRL, a rehearsal method, is effective in the most challenging Class-IL. They state that Task-IL scenarios may surprisingly not be as easy to learn for DP as for other domains.
quotes: We found that though regularization-based methods performed
well in Data-IL and Domain-IL, only iCaRL, a rehearsal method, is eﬀective in the most challenging Class-IL.
Surprisingly, Task-IL scenarios may not be as easy to learn for DP as for other domains.
assertions.reader_inference: Table S1 does not clearly show regularization methods performing well: in Data-IL, EWC (86.77) and Online EWC (83.29) are below finetuning (88.49), and in Domain-IL the regularization methods (63.64 to 67.51) are 22 to 26 points below Joint (89.43). The Task-IL remark rests on the Task-IL finetuning and CL accuracies not exceeding finetuning.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference 28, that the FDA has not approved algorithms based on CL, and that extensive research is needed to establish regulations for safely incorporating CL in clinical settings. They state that their evaluation approaches and method to generate domain-shifted datasets can potentially serve as a first step towards this goal.
quotes: FDA has not approved algorithms based on CL [28] and extensive research is needed to establish regulations for safely incorporating CL in clinical settings.
Our evaluation approaches and proposed method to generate domain-shifted datasets can potentially serve as the ﬁrst step towards this goal.
assertions.reader_inference: Time-sensitive: the regulatory status is as of the 2021 Lancet Digital Health commentary (reference 28) and the 2022 preprint; it should not be read as current.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that they evaluated CL methods in an online few-shot setting under the constraints of annotation and computational resources, and that they revealed promising results of CL in DP applications, potentially paving the way for application of these methods in clinical practice.
quotes: In addition, we evaluated CL methods in an online few-shot setting under the constraints of annotation and computational resources.
We revealed promising results of CL in DP applications, potentially paving the way for application of these methods in clinical practice.
assertions.reader_inference: The body of the paper never uses the term few-shot and does not describe an experiment with reduced annotation; its online experiments use A-GEM and CoPE with 1 epoch and mini experiences of 128 samples. The online results are mixed (A-GEM and CoPE below or near finetuning in most scenarios), so 'promising results' is the authors' framing.
